title: Anatomy of a painting
summary: Support, ground, underdrawing, paint, glaze, varnish — the stack a forger has to fake, layer by layer.

shots.title:
A painting is
a stack.
shots.subtitle: Support, ground, drawing, paint, varnish.
shots.narration: A painting is not just a picture on a surface. It is a stack of layers, each with its own materials and its own history — and a forger has to fake every one.
From the bottom: a support, a ground that prepares it, an underdrawing, layers of paint, perhaps transparent glazes, and on top a protective varnish.

shots.text: Panels came first. **Canvas** — hemp or flax on a wooden frame — spread later.
shots.narration: Wooden panels were the usual support before canvas: cloth of hemp or flax stretched on a wooden frame. The earliest surviving painted canvases date from the late fourteenth century.

shots.text: On panels the ground is **gesso**: gypsum in animal glue, sanded smooth.
shots.narration: The ground prepares the support. On panels it is usually gesso — gypsum bound in animal-skin glue, laid coarse, then fine, and sanded absolutely smooth.
Next, the artist drew the composition on the primed surface. That underdrawing usually disappears under the paint, but infrared imaging can bring it back.
Paint is pigment — the colour — bound in a medium. Egg tempera, oil, watercolour and glue size are all media, and each one handles differently.

right.heading: Oil
items: Used in the North from the 13th century

shots.narration: Egg tempera was the medium of most early Italian paintings and grew rarer after 1500. Oil, developed by Van Eyck and Campin, reached Italy in the early fifteenth century and dries slowly.
Varnish adds gloss and protection. Natural varnishes darken and discolour with time, which is why old pictures are periodically cleaned and varnished again.

shots.text: **Craquelure**: the cracks of age, running into the varnish.
shots.narration: As paint layers age and shrink they crack. Almost every old picture has craquelure across its whole surface — so forgers have to manufacture it.

shots.text: A **cross-section** under the microscope shows the whole stack.
shots.narration: A pinhead-sized sample, mounted and polished as a cross-section, shows every layer under the microscope and identifies the pigments — evidence that helps to date a painting.
